name: Pino de Casandra

location.address: Majada Alta, beside the Presa de las Ninas, Parque Rural del Nublo, Tejeda

verified_sources: OpenStreetMap natural=tree node named Arbol de Casandra

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: Pino de Casandra, Tejeda, visitable, access normal)

access: Free, open countryside in the Parque Rural del Nublo beside the reservoir (parking, barbecue area). Cabildo is defining and reinforcing paths under the crown to limit trampling; keep to the marked path.
transport: No practical public transport; about 1.5 hours by car from Las Palmas via GC-15, GC-600, GC-605 to the Presa de las Ninas, tree a short walk from the dam (OSM node about 230 m from the dam).
verify_notes: Alive: Cabildo watering and soil plan August 2025 (RTVC/Europa Press 2025-08-21); iNaturalist observation 2023-03-21 at the OSM node (lifecheck RECENT). Age: RTVC 'over 380 years'; Gran Canaria tourism site 'four-century old'; Barcelo guide says ~400; Komoot blurb says 500+ (not used). Size per RTVC: trunk about 2.5 m diameter at base (girth_cm = pi x 250 = 785, derived, base of trunk), 25 m tall, crown about 30 m across. Also called Pino Bonito. Survived several fires and lightning strikes, unusual shape, large burn scar. Legend of Casandra, a 15-year-old burned at the tree, no official version, tourism site says unknown whether true. Wikidata Q75754696 has pin 27.92407,-15.67228 (about 500 m off the OSM node); OSM node used because it is a named tree node near the dam coordinate 27.92793,-15.66729. Cabildo plans a permanent information table. Same Cabildo catalogue (2021) lists about 85 to 90 singular trees and 10 dragos; catalogue itself not retrieved (not fetched as a PDF). CORRECTION/UPDATE: the official Cabildo ficha gives perimeter at 1.30 m 5.30 m (girth_cm 530, used instead of the pi x 2.5 m diameter figure which RTVC quotes for the base), height 25 m, age over 380 years, ownership recorded as private, Visitable, access Normal. Ficha coordinate 27.92580,-15.66734 matches the OSM named tree node within about 5 m, so the pin is confirmed from two independent mappings.
story:
This pine is named after a girl who may never have existed. Legend says Casandra, fifteen years old, was burned at this tree. There is no official version of the story, and Gran Canaria's own tourism board says plainly that nobody knows whether any of it is true. Locals have a second, kinder name for it, the Pino Bonito, the pretty pine.

What is certain is the tree. It stands above the Presa de las Niñas reservoir in the pine country of Tejeda, inside the Parque Rural del Nublo, and the Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees puts it at over 380 years old. The tourism board rounds that to four centuries. It is 25 metres tall and 5.30 metres round at chest height, with a crown about 30 metres across.

It has come through several fires and lightning strikes, and it shows. The trunk carries a large burn scar and the whole tree has grown into a shape nobody would call regular, which is most of its appeal.

In August 2025 the Cabildo began a plan to water it and improve the soil around its roots, and it is marking out paths under the crown to limit trampling. Keep to them. There is parking and a picnic area by the dam, and the tree is a short walk away. Getting here takes about an hour and a half by car from Las Palmas, with no practical bus.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the large burn scar on a trunk 5.30 metres round, under a crown about 30 metres wide. It stands a short walk from the Presa de las Niñas dam, about 230 metres away.

name: Drago de Galdar

location.address: Courtyard of the old Casas Consistoriales (now the tourist office), Plaza de Santiago, Galdar

verified_sources: OpenStreetMap natural=tree node Drago de Galdar

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: Drago de Galdar, public, visitable, access easy)

access: Public. The tree stands in the inner courtyard of the old town hall, now the Galdar tourist office on Plaza de Santiago; Cabildo ficha: visitable, easy access. Gran Canaria tourism site gives town hall opening Monday to Friday 08:00 to 14:30. Its crown rises above the building roofline.
transport: Galdar bus station about 5 min walk; guagua lines from Las Palmas (about 50 min by car, 60 to 75 min by bus, check exact route).
verify_notes: Official Cabildo ficha (fetched): perimeter at 1.30 m 4 m (girth_cm 400), base diameter 1.40 m, height 8 m, crown 12 m, estimated age 300 years, planted 1718 per the ficha text, oldest drago on the island; ownership public; not in a protected space. Ficha coordinate 28.14460,-15.65537 matches the OSM named tree node within 1 m and an iNaturalist observation dated 2026-07-03 (lifecheck RECENT). The earlier hispanopedia figures (perimeter 2.5 m, height 8.5 m) are superseded by the ficha. Ficha story: engraved scars from historic resin (dragon's blood) tapping; legend of Dona Catalina la regannona, a Galdar noblewoman who left a convent after faking her death and worked as a herbalist beneath this drago. 2016 scale-insect infestation cut foliage about 40 percent, recovery declared in 2019 (hispanopedia). Flowered only 5 or 6 times in 77 years per its technical sheet. Municipal leaflet and tourism site agree on 1718. Part of the Conjunto Historico-Artistico of Plaza de Santiago (1981) with the Iglesia de Santiago de los Caballeros. Not the 50-year-old drago felled in La Vega, Galdar, in 2025.
story:
Gran Canaria's oldest dragon tree lives in a town hall courtyard, and it has outgrown the building. The Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees dates the Drago de Gáldar to 1718, which makes it about 300 years old, and the town's own leaflet gives the same year.

It is 8 metres tall and 4 metres round at chest height, with a crown 12 metres across that rises above the roofline of the old Casas Consistoriales, now the tourist office on the Plaza de Santiago. The trunk still carries engraved scars from the centuries when people tapped it for its red resin, sold as dragon's blood.

It also carries a legend. Doña Catalina, remembered in Gáldar as la regañona, the scold, was a noblewoman said to have faked her own death to get out of a convent and then to have lived as a herbalist beneath this tree.

Its recent history is less romantic. In 2016 a scale insect infestation cost it about 40 percent of its foliage, and recovery was only declared in 2019. It flowers rarely, five or six times in 77 years according to its technical sheet, so nobody should plan a trip around the blossom.

The square around it, with the church of Santiago de los Caballeros, has been a protected historic ensemble since 1981. The courtyard keeps office hours, Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 14:30 by the island tourism board's listing, and the bus station is five minutes away on foot.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, 12 metres across, showing above the roof of the old town hall. It stands in the inner courtyard of the tourist office on the Plaza de Santiago.

name: Araucaria of the Plaza de Teror

location.address: Plaza de Nuestra Senora del Pino, beside the basilica and the Casas Consistoriales, Teror

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: Araucaria de la Plaza de Teror, public, visitable, easy)

access: Free, in the public square beside the Basilica de Nuestra Senora del Pino; open at all times.
transport: Bus (guagua) from Las Palmas to Teror, about 40 to 50 min by road, check line; tree is in the central plaza.
verify_notes: One official register (Cabildo ficha) plus lifecheck RECENT (iNaturalist observation within 10 m); register only for age. Ficha: 38 m tall, trunk perimeter over 5 m, estimated age over 100 years (no planting date). Two parallel trunks fork low, the main trunk probably truncated by a storm or lightning early in the 20th century; the ficha says this multi-stem form is its main singularity. A stone bench at its base, popularly called 'el queque', where townspeople gather. The ficha says at least ten large araucarias stand around Teror, this being the one in the square. Ficha coordinate 28.05928,-15.54806 sits at the plaza next to the basilica (OSM basilica node 28.05930,-15.54781). Plaza also tied to the Pino de la Virgen legend: the image of the Virgin found in a pine in 1481, the original Pino de las Maravillas fell, no living tree is claimed to be it (the Cabildo catalogues a Pino de la Virgen in Teror, but only about 70 years old, so not ancient). Flagged: register-only for age and age is a bound, not an estimate.
story:
Teror's basilica is named after a pine, and the tallest tree beside it is not a true pine at all. By tradition an image of the Virgin was found in a pine tree here in 1481, and the church became Nuestra Señora del Pino. That original tree, the Pino de las Maravillas, fell, and no living tree in the square claims to be it.

What towers over the plaza now is a Norfolk Island Pine, an araucaria from the South Pacific, 38 metres tall and more than 5 metres round. The Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees estimates it at over 100 years old. Treat that as a floor rather than a date. Nobody has recorded when it was planted, and the catalogue is the only source for its age.

The catalogue says its real distinction is its shape. Two parallel trunks rise from a low fork, and the main trunk was probably cut short by a storm or lightning early in the twentieth century. Whatever took the top off, the tree has kept climbing.

At its foot is a stone bench the town calls el queque, where people sit and meet, which makes this as much a piece of Teror's daily life as of its scenery. The catalogue counts at least ten large araucarias around Teror; this is the one in the square, open at all hours. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two parallel trunks forking low, 38 metres to the top, with a stone bench at its foot. It stands in the plaza beside the Basilica de Nuestra Señora del Pino.

name: Drago de Pino Santo

location.address: Barranco Alonso (Hoya Bravo), Pino Santo, Santa Brigida; seen from the GC-151 road to Pino Santo

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: Drago de Pino Santo), also in the Santa Brigida municipal catalogue since 2008

access: VIEW ONLY. Private land (ficha: not visitable). It stands on a basalt cliff about 15 m above the Barranco Alonso and can be seen from the GC-151 road that leads to Pino Santo, or from the barranco floor. Do not enter the finca.
transport: Car or guagua towards Pino Santo, Santa Brigida (about 25 min from Las Palmas by car); the GC-151 viewpoint is by the road.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree: Cabildo ficha (height 16 m, perimeter at 1.30 m 4.9 m, about 240 to 250 years from 15 branchings, in good condition) and RTVC 2021-03-18 (17 m tall, crown 15 m, 240 years, fifth oldest tree on the island per the Cabildo, 'el rey de los dragos de Gran Canaria'; cochineal/lapilla infestation yellowed about a quarter of the crown, treated June 2020 in four rounds from a crane, brought under control; Cabildo keeps monitoring). The ficha says it is the most spectacular wild-looking tree on the island, dramatic on the cliff, frames a garden like Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, worry that the rock could one day give way. Flowered only 5 or 6 times in the last 77 years (geographer Rafael S. Almeida), about once per 14 years. Alive: iNaturalist observation within 10 m (lifecheck RECENT). Ficha coordinate 28.03262,-15.51322 within about 20 m of Wikidata Q124100237 (28.03278,-15.51319); unique crown on the cliff so pin is confirmed. Also known as Drago de Barranco Alonso or de Hoya Bravo. Included in the 100 singular trees of Macaronesia (Canarias7 2021). Private land: access is view-only from the road.
story:
The biggest dragon tree on Gran Canaria grows on a basalt cliff, about 15 metres above the floor of the Barranco Alonso, and you can only look at it from across the way. RTVC, the Canary Islands broadcaster, calls it the king of the island's dragos.

The Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees gives it 16 metres of height (RTVC says 17), a trunk 4.9 metres round at chest height and a crown about 15 metres wide. Its age is counted from its 15 branchings, which puts it at roughly 240 to 250 years. RTVC, quoting the Cabildo, ranks it the fifth oldest tree on the island.

The catalogue drops its usual dry tone for this one. It calls it the most spectacular wild-looking tree on Gran Canaria, framing the garden below like a scene from Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, and it admits a worry that the rock holding it could one day give way.

In 2020 a cochineal infestation turned about a quarter of the crown yellow. The Cabildo treated it in four rounds from a crane that June and brought the plague under control, and it still keeps watch. It is also counted among the 100 singular trees of Macaronesia.

The tree stands on private land and the finca is not open. See it from the GC-151 road that climbs to Pino Santo, or from the floor of the barranco, about 25 minutes by car from Las Palmas.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone dragon tree on the basalt cliff, about 15 metres above the Barranco Alonso, its crown 15 metres wide. You see it from the GC-151 road to Pino Santo; the land is private.

name: Drago del Jardin de la Marquesa

location.address: Jardin de la Marquesa (Jardin de las Hesperides), road between Arucas and Banaderos, Arucas

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: public garden, visitable, easy)

access: Historic garden open to the public since 1985 (ficha: visitable, easy access). Opening hours and entry fee not established in this pass; check before visiting.
transport: Between Arucas and Banaderos on the Vega road, about 25 min by car from Las Palmas; bus Arucas to Banaderos, check line.
verify_notes: One official register (Cabildo ficha): height 10 m, perimeter at 1.30 m 4.3 m, base diameter 1.6 m, crown 14 m, 15 branchings, about 230 years (the text says about 250), predates the colonial palace built 1880 by the Marques Ramon Madan y Uriondo. The ficha says it outclasses two other centenarian dragos at the garden entrance, so the trunk worth the visit is the large one among three. Alive: iNaturalist observation within 10 m (lifecheck RECENT). Ficha coordinate 28.12467,-15.52869 not checked on the crown; pin approximate within the garden. Flagged: register only, access hours and fee missing, pin not tied to one of three dragos by a mapped photo. The same ficha mentions an eucalyptus called Arbol Bonito (Marquesa de Arucas) between Arucas and Banaderos, a possible lead.
story:
This dragon tree is older than the palace it now decorates. When the Marqués Ramón Madan y Uriondo built his colonial palace between Arucas and Bañaderos in 1880, this drago was already standing, according to the Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees.

The catalogue cannot quite settle on its age. Its figures say about 230 years, its text says about 250, both counted from the tree's 15 branchings, so somewhere between the two is the honest answer. It is 10 metres tall and 4.3 metres round at chest height, with a base 1.6 metres across and a crown spreading 14 metres.

There are three dragon trees here, which matters if you want the right one. Two centenarian dragos stand at the garden entrance, and the catalogue says this one outclasses them both. Look for the largest of the three.

The Jardín de la Marquesa, also called the Jardín de las Hespérides, has been open to the public since 1985. We have not confirmed its current hours or entry fee, so check before you go. It sits on the Vega road about 25 minutes by car from Las Palmas, with a bus from Arucas towards Bañaderos.

The same catalogue lists a eucalyptus nearby known as the Árbol Bonito. If you have seen it, tell us where it stands.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the largest of the three dragon trees in the Jardín de la Marquesa, 4.3 metres round with a 14 metre crown. The two smaller ones stand at the garden entrance.

name: Sabina de Tirma

location.address: Casas de Tirma, Finca de Tirma, beside the Barranco de las Casillas (Los Pilones), Parque Natural de Tamadaba, Agaete

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares de Gran Canaria, Cabildo de Gran Canaria (ficha: Sabina de Tirma, Agaete, public, visitable, access normal)

access: Public land inside the Parque Natural de Tamadaba (ficha: Publico, Visitable, access Normal). Reached by the GC-216 mountain road; the Cabildo's marked footpath S-94 (Portada de Tirma, La Marquesa, El Risco de Agaete) starts in the area. No opening hours or fee published for the Casas de Tirma; precise last stretch on foot not established.
transport: No practical public transport. By car about 1h15 from Las Palmas via Agaete or via Artenara on the GC-216, to the Tirma forest houses; the tree is at the Casas de Tirma beside the barranco.
verify_notes: Cabildo ficha (fetched 2026-11-02): ficha text says one of the largest and oldest sabinas in the Canaries, 16 m tall, age could reach 400 to 500 years, basal perimeter 4 m (ficha table: perimeter at 1.30 m 4.40 m, base diameter 1.90 m, diameter at 1.30 m 1.40 m), three thick trunks, one torn and now propped on a wall built by estate workers in 1995. Oral tradition: a raven came to drink at the slope and left the seed that grew into the tree. Cabildo geographer census (Cabrera Mujica) counts about 300 wild sabinas on the island. PIN: three coordinates within about 11 m agree: ficha 28.03348,-15.72668; OSM natural=tree node 5301140203 at 28.0333841,-15.7266875 (denotation natural_monument, unnamed); iNaturalist observation 256910071 Juniperus canariensis 2024-12-31 at 28.0334625,-15.7266426. OSM node used. Confirmed. ALIVE: iNaturalist 2024-12-31 (less than two years ago, same trunk by coordinate). Sources: one official register plus an observation; register age is the Cabildo's estimate. Flagged: no second descriptive source found (web search found nothing independent on this tree); access last stretch and hours not verified (OSM access tags not read, Overpass mirror timed out twice). Almacigos de Tirma (mastic trees) stand at the same site per the earlier pass; iNaturalist 2024-12-31 has Pistacia atlantica 35 to 40 m from the sabina. Ficha height 16 m, girth 440 cm at 1.30 m (figure from the Cabildo, use as is).
story:
A raven planted this juniper, if you ask the people of Tirma. By their oral tradition the bird came down to drink on the slope and left behind the seed. The Cabildo's catalogue of singular trees sticks to measurements, and calls it one of the largest and oldest sabinas in the Canary Islands.

It stands 16 metres tall at the Casas de Tirma, beside the Barranco de las Casillas in the Parque Natural de Tamadaba, high above Agaete. The trunk is 4.40 metres round at chest height. The catalogue estimates that it could reach 400 to 500 years, and that estimate is the only one there is.

It grows as three thick trunks. One of them tore away from the others, and in 1995 the workers on the estate built a wall to hold it up. It is propped on that wall now.

Trees like this are scarce on Gran Canaria. A census by the Cabildo's geographers counts about 300 wild sabinas left on the whole island. A mastic tree, one of the almácigos de Tirma, grows about 35 metres away.

There is no practical bus. By car it is about an hour and a quarter from Las Palmas on the GC-216 mountain road, through Agaete or Artenara, to the forest houses at Tirma. The Cabildo's marked footpath S-94 starts in the same area. No hours are published for the Casas de Tirma, so plan the last stretch on foot from a map before you set out.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its three thick trunks, one of them torn away and propped on a wall built in 1995. It stands at the Casas de Tirma, beside the Barranco de las Casillas.

name: Rubber figs of Parque de San Telmo

location.address: Parque de San Telmo, Triana, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria

verified_sources: https://lpgcsostenible.laspalmasgc.es/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Catalogo_arboles_LPGC.pdf (ficha ARB-068, pp. 204-205 of the document; the Ayuntamiento's Catalogo de arboles singulares y conjuntos arboreos, December 2024)

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares y Conjuntos Arboreos de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Ayuntamiento (ficha ARB-068, public garden square; the three figs also belong to conjunto CON-02, Parque de San Telmo)

access: Free, public garden square (ficha: titularidad publica, plaza ajardinada), open at all times as far as sources say; no hours published.
transport: San Telmo is the city's central bus (guagua) station area, next to the park; Triana shopping street is beside it. Flat, city centre.
verify_notes: Ficha ARB-068 (PDF fetched 2026-11-02): Ficus macrophylla, 3 specimens, the oldest of the species in the park. Heights 11 / 12 / 14 m; trunk perimeters 3.00 + 1.90 / 2.17 + 2.45 / 3.27 m (multi-stem, so girth_cm 327 is the single largest stem only); base perimeters 4.00 / 5.00 / 2.00 m; crown diameters 20 / 17 / 19 m, projections 315 / 240 / 295 m2; age estimate '+- 150/200 years' (authors' estimate); criterion historical and landscape. Ficha says they may come from the 1840 project for the new alameda-paseo in northern Triana (planos de Domingo Rancel), 'quizas', so planting date NOT stated; do not bridge. Ficha advises a stability study of the branches because the area is heavily used. Photos in ficha September 2020 only. Ficha coordinate (UTM 28N X459024.83 Y3109271.20, converted) = 28.10831,-15.41716, ONE coordinate for three trees, so pin approximate at the group; Commons geotags in the park (GC Las Palmas San Telmo R01/R02) are at 18 m but are park-level. ALIVE: lifecheck OLD (Commons 2012); only the ficha photographs (2020) and the catalogue's own fieldwork (published December 2024) support it. Flagged for alive-recency and register-only. Not verified by a second source. The same park conjunto CON-02 also lists a Lagunaria patersonia ARB-093 (14 m, 2.60 m, +-75/100 years, 28.10926,-15.41711), a Phoenix reclinata ARB-150 and a pica-pica; a recognise-line writer should say which of the three figs is biggest (14 m, 3.27 m stem).
story:
Three figs, each with a crown up to 20 metres wide, shade the park beside the main bus station of Las Palmas. They are Moreton Bay figs, a species from eastern Australia, and the city's catalogue of singular trees names them the oldest of their kind in the Parque de San Telmo.

The catalogue's authors estimate them at roughly 150 to 200 years. They wonder, with a careful "perhaps", whether the figs go back to the 1840 plan for a new promenade in the north of Triana, drawn by Domingo Rancel. Nobody has recorded when they were actually planted.

They are listed together as one group, and it is worth standing under all three. Their heights run 11, 12 and 14 metres and their crowns spread 20, 17 and 19 metres. Two of them split into a pair of stems, and the base of one is 5 metres round.

The park is heavily used, and for that reason the catalogue recommends a study of how stable the big branches are. If you walk through and find them changed, tell us.

San Telmo sits at the north end of Triana, the old shopping street, with the city's central guagua station beside it. Entry is free and the ground is flat. From here the walk south into Vegueta passes the Árbol del Responso, an ombu on Juan de Quesada and a dragon tree by a covered fountain.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise the biggest of the three by its single trunk, 3.27 metres round, rising to 14 metres. They stand together in the Parque de San Telmo, the oldest figs in the park.

name: Arbol del Responso

location.address: Plaza Nuestra Senora de Los Reyes (roundabout), Vegueta, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria

verified_sources: https://lpgcsostenible.laspalmasgc.es/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Catalogo_arboles_LPGC.pdf (ficha ARB-070, pp. 208-209 of the document; Ayuntamiento catalogue, December 2024)

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares y Conjuntos Arboreos de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Ayuntamiento (ficha ARB-070, public roundabout)

access: Free, public roundabout garden on a street square; can be seen from the pavement at all times. Traffic roundabout, so view from the edge.
transport: Vegueta, about 10 to 15 min on foot south of the Plaza de Santa Ana cathedral square; city buses stop in Vegueta (lines not checked). About 1.5 km on foot from Parque de San Telmo.
verify_notes: Ficha ARB-070 (PDF fetched 2026-11-02): Ficus macrophylla, known as 'Arbol del Responso'; height 10.20 m, trunk 1.80 m clear, perimeter at trunk 3.80 m (girth_cm 380), base perimeter 4.10 m, crown 11.70 m (107 m2), age estimate +-125/150 years (authors' estimate); criterion historical, cultural, landscape. History per ficha: around 1833 the British colony asked the council for land to bury its dead, so the Vegueta cemetery took in other faiths; Protestant rites were held at an enormous Indian laurel on the road to the cemetery (the 'responso' tree). In 2002 urban works 'moved' this historic fig about a hundred metres, ending the traditional use (the ficha says moved; whether a transplant of the live tree or a replacement is not stated, so keep wording as the ficha has it). Ficha photograph May 2023. Coordinate: UTM 28N X459225.69 Y3107901.84 converted = 28.09596,-15.41507, a surveyed single-tree coordinate (the survey of Vegueta-Triana by MDT Topografia); pin confirmed from the register's own tree-level survey, not independently cross-checked (no OSM name, no iNaturalist or tree-specific Commons geotag found). Alive: ficha photograph May 2023 (about 3.5 years), catalogue field work to 2024/25; lifecheck not run on this tree. Flagged: register only, alive evidence over two years old, ficha says the tree was moved in 2002 (age counts the tree, not the spot). Mid-list of the Vegueta-Triana walk, about 1.5 km from San Telmo.
story:
This fig is named after a funeral prayer. The responso is the short prayer said over the dead, and for the Protestants of Las Palmas it was said under a great tree on the road to the cemetery.

The story, as the city's catalogue of singular trees tells it, begins around 1833, when the British colony asked the council for ground to bury its dead. The Vegueta cemetery was opened to other faiths, and Protestant rites were held at an enormous tree on the way there. That tree became the Árbol del Responso.

In 2002 street works moved this historic fig about a hundred metres, and the old custom ended with the move. The catalogue estimates the fig now standing in the Plaza Nuestra Señora de Los Reyes at roughly 125 to 150 years, an estimate by its own authors, so whether this is the tree of the first Protestant funerals is a question the record does not answer. If you know, tell us.

What you see today is a Moreton Bay fig 10.20 metres tall, with a trunk 3.80 metres round that runs clear for 1.80 metres before it branches, and a crown nearly 12 metres across. It grows in the garden of a traffic roundabout, so look from the pavement at the edge rather than crossing to it.

It is about 10 to 15 minutes on foot south of the cathedral square of Santa Ana, and about 1.5 kilometres from the figs of San Telmo.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big fig in the roundabout garden, 3.80 metres round with a clear trunk of 1.80 metres. It stands in the Plaza Nuestra Señora de Los Reyes, in Vegueta.

name: Ombu of Juan de Quesada

location.address: Calle Juan de Quesada, 1, side bed of the street, Vegueta, Las Palmas de Gran Canaria

verified_sources: https://lpgcsostenible.laspalmasgc.es/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Catalogo_arboles_LPGC.pdf (ficha ARB-154, pp. 394-395 of the document; Ayuntamiento catalogue, December 2024)

official_register.name: Catalogo de Arboles Singulares y Conjuntos Arboreos de Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Ayuntamiento (ficha ARB-154; also part of conjunto CON-01 Juan de Quesada)

access: Free, public pavement bed beside the street, visible at all times.
transport: Vegueta, a few minutes on foot from the Plaza de Santa Ana; about 800 m on foot from Parque de San Telmo.
verify_notes: Ficha ARB-154 (PDF fetched 2026-11-02): Phytolacca dioica, ombu or 'bellasombra', from South America; height 10 m, clear trunk 3 m, trunk perimeter 2.40 m (girth_cm 240), base perimeter 6.00 m (the swollen buttress base), crown 10 m (83 m2); age estimate +-100/125 years (authors' estimate); criterion historical, landscape and sociocultural; in a side bed of the street. Ficha story: in the 1950s the city's chief gardener Juan Gonzalez ('Juanito Ficus') removed many big trees of the city for damage to roads and pavements but kept a few, this one acting as a landscape marker for the area; Kunkel (1969) also cites it; it needs its base freed of asphalt. Ficha photographs 2014, October 2018 and October 2020. Coordinate: UTM 28N X459144.02 Y3108516.49 converted = 28.10150,-15.41592, a surveyed single-tree coordinate; lifecheck RECENT hit (iNaturalist 2024-01-18) is a eucalyptus 16 m away, not this tree, so no independent alive proof. Pin confirmed from the register tree-level survey only. Flagged: register only, last dated photograph October 2020. Other Vegueta trees within 100 m on the same street (Conjunto Juan de Quesada CON-01): a 40 m Araucaria columnaris ARB-001 (private garden), Syzygium cumini ARB-170, Washingtonia ARB-173.
story:
In the 1950s the head gardener of Las Palmas cut down many of the city's big trees, and this one he chose to keep. Juan González, remembered by the nickname Juanito Ficus, took out trees that were breaking up roads and pavements, the city's catalogue of singular trees records, but spared a few. This ombu was one, kept as a landmark for the street.

The ombu comes from South America, and in Spanish it also goes by bellasombra, beautiful shade. Its trunk is 2.40 metres round, but the swollen foot it stands on measures 6 metres. It rises 10 metres to a crown about as wide.

The catalogue's authors estimate it at roughly 100 to 125 years. Kunkel already cited it in his work of 1969. The same catalogue says the base needs to be freed of the asphalt around it. If you pass and find it changed, tell us.

It grows in a side bed of Calle Juan de Quesada, in Vegueta, a few minutes on foot from the Plaza de Santa Ana and about 800 metres from the Parque de San Telmo. The same short street holds other catalogued trees, among them a 40 metre araucaria in a private garden.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the swollen base, 6 metres round, below a trunk of 2.40 metres. It stands in the side bed of Calle Juan de Quesada at number 1, in Vegueta.

story:
This dragon tree leans, and since 2017 it has had help staying up. The city's catalogue of singular trees records a support system fitted that year to keep it from falling over as its tilt grows, and says the props should be reviewed.

By the island's standards it is young. Gran Canaria's oldest dragos, at Gáldar, Pino Santo and Arucas, are put at 230 to 300 years. This one has branched six times, which the catalogue reads as about 100 years. It is 7.80 metres tall, with a trunk 1.70 metres round that runs clear for 4.40 metres before the first fork and a small crown about 4 metres across.

The reason to stop is the square around it. The Plaza del Espíritu Santo, in Vegueta, holds a small hermitage and a covered monumental fountain of 1862 by the Gran Canaria artist Manuel Ponce de León Falcón, restored in 1993. Writing in 1956, Lola de la Torre described the garden of palms here as being like an oasis that hides the hermitage. A Mexican fan palm 23 metres tall stands about 10 metres from the drago.

It is five to ten minutes on foot from the cathedral square of Santa Ana and about 900 metres from the Parque de San Telmo, which makes it an easy stop on a walk through Vegueta's old trees. The garden is free and can be seen from the square.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the lean and the supports holding it, on a trunk that runs clear for 4.40 metres. It stands in the garden of the Plaza del Espíritu Santo, about 10 metres from a 23 metre fan palm.
